extracted.intended_audience: Florida citizens, regulated parties, agency staff, JAPC/DOAH personnel, and attorneys involved in Florida administrative rulemaking and challenges
extracted.subtask_description: A pocket guide summarizing Chapter 120, Florida Statutes: definitions, procedural requirements, timelines, notice contents, cost analyses, review roles (JAPC, DOAH), and remedies for rulemaking, rule challenges, licensing, variances, exemptions, and related agency actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rule" means each agency statement of general applicability that implements, interprets, or prescribes law or policy or agency statements describing the procedure or practice requirements of the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effect of an agency statement, not the agency’s characterization of its actions, determines if it is a rule. Includes amendment or repeal of a rule. Criteria not disclosed while enforcing statutory requirements are rules. Agency forms imposing requirements or soliciting information not specifically required by statute or existing rule are rules. Certain internal management memoranda not affecting private interests or having application outside the agency are statutorily exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Statutory Authority for Rulemaking (Map-Tack §120.536(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may adopt only those rules that implement or interpret the specific powers and duties granted by the enabling statute; a grant of rulemaking authority alone is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must 'pinpoint' the particular statute being implemented. Rules may not enlarge, modify, or contravene the provisions of law they implement. The provision was enacted to prevent rules adopted on broad grants of authority without specific statutory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for Invalidity of a Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule may be invalid if it: enlarges/modifies/contravenes the law; exceeds statutory rulemaking authority; is arbitrary or capricious; is vague or does not establish adequate standards; vests unbridled discretion in the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also invalid if it adds additional criteria beyond governing statute or imposes regulatory costs that could be reduced by less costly alternatives. Emergency rules can be invalid if no emergency exists, if the agency exceeded its statutory authority, or if not promulgated in compliance with §120.54(4), F.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking Procedural Steps (§120.54)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical procedural sequence for adopting a rule: draft and agency head approval; notice of rule development; publish notice of proposed rulemaking in FAR; submit copy and materials to JAPC at least 21 days prior to adoption; respond to JAPC; hold hearing if requested within 21 days; publish notice(s) of change or withdrawal; JAPC certification; file for adoption with Department of State; rule effective per statutory timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: notice of rule development is required unless repealing; JAPC reviews and consults with agency; agency must file with Department of State; rule becomes effective 20 days after filing (or later if specified). If agency postpones adoption for JAPC review the normal 90-day filing period is tolled.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAR Notice Content Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Florida Administrative Register (FAR), the notice must include specified elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements include: a short, plain explanation of purpose/effect; proposed rule number; full text of proposed rule or amendment and a summary; reference to grant of rulemaking authority; reference to Florida Statutes or Laws being implemented/interpreted; contact name/e-mail/phone; concise summary of SERC if prepared; agency website where full SERC can be viewed (if prepared); statement that any person may provide information or a proposal for a lower cost regulatory alternative within 21 days; statement whether legislative ratification is expected to be required; and description of procedure for requesting a public hearing. Notices of proposed rulemaking must be published within 180 days after the most recent notice of rule development unless a concise statement of reasons for delay is filed with JAPC at least 7 days before the end of the 180-day period. Notices must be published at least 7 days after notice of rule development and at least 28 days prior to intended action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and Deadline Requirements for Rulemaking and Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple statutory deadlines govern notice publication, JAPC submission, indexing, and effective dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: submit rule and supporting materials to JAPC at least 21 days prior to adoption; hearing requested within 21 days after publication triggers a hearing; publish notices of change at least 21 days prior to adoption; publish notices of correction at least 7 days prior; JAPC must be notified 7 days prior to adoption if there are no changes; agency files rule for adoption and rule becomes effective 20 days after filing (or later as specified). Rules must be indexed within 90 days after filing; orders must be electronically submitted to a centralized database within 90 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Estimated Regulatory Costs (SERC) — Triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to adoption/amendment/repeal of any rule (other than emergency rules), an agency must prepare a SERC if the proposed rule will have a negative impact on small business or is likely to directly or indirectly increase total regulatory costs in excess of $200,000 within one year after implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a substantially affected person submits a good faith written proposal for a lower cost regulatory alternative within 21 days after publication, the agency must prepare or revise its SERC and either adopt the alternative or explain reasons for rejecting it. Agencies must also revise SERC if any change increases regulatory costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: SERC — Required Contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A SERC must include specified economic analyses, estimates, and descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must include: an economic analysis assessing whether the rule is likely to have negative impacts on economic growth, business competitiveness, or increased regulatory costs exceeding $1 million within 5 years; a good faith estimate of number of individuals/entities likely required to comply and description of types; estimate of cost to agency/state/local governments for implementation/enforcement including revenue effects; estimate of direct costs to regulated persons (fees, equipment, reporting, etc.); analysis of impact on small counties/cities and small businesses and basis for decision not to implement less costly alternatives; market impacts (changes to customer charges, market value, substitution costs, reasonable value of time to understand/comply); description of any regulatory alternatives submitted and agency's adoption/rejection reasons; any additional useful information the agency determines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative Ratification Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule is likely to have an adverse impact on economic growth > $1 million in 5 years, adversely affect business competitiveness > $1 million in 5 years, or increase regulatory costs > $1 million in 5 years, the rule must be ratified (approved) by the Legislature before taking effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must notify JAPC within 3 days after submitting a rule to the Legislature for ratification. Exemptions include emergency rules, rules adopting federal standards, and rules specifically exempted by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Rule Adoption Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may adopt emergency rules when authorized; most general rulemaking requirements do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency rules generally effective for a maximum of 90 days and are not renewable, except when a proposed rule addressing the subject is pending and challenged or requires legislative ratification. Emergency rules are not subject to the usual SERC and many other general requirements, but may be challenged if no emergency exists or procedures were not followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and Centralized Access (FAC and FAR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and notices must be published and made available in single sources: the Florida Administrative Register (FAR) and Florida Administrative Code (FAC), maintained by the Administrative Code and Register Section of the Department of State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAR notifies the public of proposed rule development, proposed rulemaking (including text), changes/corrections, withdrawals, scheduled meetings/hearings/workshops, rules adopted during the preceding week, and dispositions of petitions. The Department is directed to publish all rules adopted by agencies, an index to rules, and history notes (including JAPC objections) in the FAC. Both FAR and FAC are available at flrules.org.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and Recordkeeping Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency must make all rules, orders, a subject-matter index of orders issued before July 1, 2015, and a list of orders not required to be indexed available for public inspection; rules must be indexed within 90 days after filing; orders electronically submitted to a centralized database within 90 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements ensure public availability and facilitate judicial and legislative oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: JAPC Review Responsibilities and Powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Joint Administrative Procedures Committee (JAPC) reviews all proposed rules and may review existing rules to determine whether they are within delegated legislative authority and conform to rulemaking procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JAPC examines rules for technical and substantive errors, consults with the agency, issues written comments, may prepare a recommended objection, and present objections in public forum. JAPC may seek judicial review on behalf of citizens for rules to which it has objected and which agencies refuse to change. JAPC may recommend suspension or sponsor legislation to address unauthorized rules. JAPC certifies to Department of State whether agency responded to all written comments prior to filing for adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: JAPC Objection and Suspension Process
rubrics_metrics.description: If JAPC votes to object to a rule, the agency may agree to amend/repeal or refuse; JAPC may request temporary suspension or prepare legislation to modify/suspend/adopt changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If agency refuses to act within 60 days or fails to proceed in good faith, JAPC may recommend a bill to modify or suspend the rule; rule suspension provisions require passage of general bill and have not been utilized historically. Objections are noted in rule history notes in FAC.

rubrics_metrics.name: JAPC Review Checklist (What JAPC examines)
rubrics_metrics.description: JAPC is required to examine whether a rule: is an invalid exercise of delegated authority; has statutory authority repealed; reiterates or paraphrases statutory material; is in proper form; had sufficient notice; is consistent with legislative intent; is necessary; could be made more comprehensible; is a reasonable implementation considering convenience; imposes regulatory costs that could be reduced by less costly alternatives; will require additional appropriations; and for emergency rules, whether an emergency exists, scope exceeded, and compliance with §120.54(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a comprehensive checklist JAPC applies when reviewing proposed, existing, and emergency rules and accompanying materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule Challenge Procedure and Burdens (DOAH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person substantially affected by a proposed or existing rule may file a petition seeking an administrative determination of its invalidity with the Division of Administrative Hearings (DOAH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For existing rules the challenger has the burden of proof; for proposed rules the agency must prove the rule is not an invalid exercise of delegated legislative authority. DOAH administrative law judges hear challenges and issue final orders; an agency may not adopt a proposed rule until the ALJ has entered a final order. DOAH forwards copies of petitions and final orders to JAPC. ALJ orders may be appealed to district courts of appeal. If a proposed rule (or portion) is declared invalid, it must be withdrawn and notice given in the FAR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unadopted Agency Policy — When It Must Be Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency statement meets the definition of a rule, the agency is required to adopt it through formal rulemaking; agency statements used to enforce statutory requirements without disclosure are rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any person substantially affected by an agency statement that should have been adopted as a rule may file a petition with DOAH seeking a determination that the statement is a rule and that the agency violated §120.54(1)(a). The APA imposes a significant burden on an agency to prove its unadopted policy is not an invalid exercise of delegated authority; if found to violate §120.54(1)(a) the agency may not rely on the statement for agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to Initiate Rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §120.54(7), any person regulated by an agency or who has a substantial interest in an agency’s rule may petition the agency to adopt, amend, or repeal a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must respond in writing either agreeing to initiate rulemaking or denying the petition; this response is a final action appealable under §120.68. If the petition relates to an agency statement not adopted as a rule and the agency does not initiate rulemaking after a public hearing, the agency must publish its reasons in the FAR, file the statement with JAPC, and JAPC or oversight committees may hold hearings and recommend legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency declaratory statement clarifies the agency’s interpretation of a statute, rule, or order as applied to a petitioner's individual situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must publish each petition for a declaratory statement and its disposition in the FAR as required by §120.565. A declaratory statement is a final agency action subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing Timeframes and Default Licensure
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, agencies have specific timeframes to act on license applications and must provide notice regarding administrative and judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon receipt of an application an agency has 30 days to examine and notify the applicant of errors/omissions or request additional permitted information. License applications must be approved or denied within 90 days of the original application or the agency’s request for additional information; this period may be tolled by initiation of administrative proceedings under §120.57. Failure to respond within prescribed time results in default licensure provided applicant meets statutory requirements and exams. Before revoking/suspending/amending/withdrawing a license the agency must notify licensee by personal service or certified mail and the licensee may request a hearing. Agencies may summarily suspend a license if immediate serious danger to public health/safety/welfare exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variances and Waivers (§120.542)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may grant variances and waivers from rule requirements to avoid unreasonable, unfair, and unintended results when statutory criteria are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A citizen must demonstrate that the rule would 'create a substantial hardship or would violate principles of fairness' and that the person can meet the purpose of the underlying statute by other means. Agencies may not grant variances/waivers to statutes. A copy of both the petition and the agency’s order granting or denying must be filed with JAPC and must include facts/reasons supporting the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from APA Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: At the request of an agency, the Administration Commission (Governor and Cabinet) may grant an exemption from any APA requirement under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include conflict with federal law/rule or necessity to obtain tax benefits or federal funds. The Commission must establish alternative procedures consistent with the intent of the APA. An order granting/denying an exemption and specifying alternatives is provided to JAPC and published in the FAR. If granted, exemptions and alternative procedures terminate 90 days following adjournment sine die of either the current or next regular legislative session after granting, or on effective date of related legislation, whichever is earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Code and Register Section Duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Code and Register Section of the Department of State publishes the FAR and the FAC and makes them available online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAR serves to notify the public of proposed rule development, proposed rulemaking text, changes/corrections, withdrawals, scheduled meetings/hearings/workshops, rules adopted during the preceding week, and disposition of petitions for administrative determinations and declaratory statements. Section 120.55(1)(a) directs the Department to publish in the FAC all rules adopted by agencies, an index to rules, and history notes including JAPC objections as authorized in §120.545(7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing Request and Challenge Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantially affected person may file a petition challenging the validity of a rule and request a hearing by an administrative law judge of DOAH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must hold a hearing if requested within 21 days after publication of the notice. If a proposed rule is challenged, the agency bears the burden to prove the rule is not an invalid exercise of delegated authority. DOAH petitions must be forwarded to JAPC; ALJ final orders are sent to JAPC and may be appealed to district courts of appeal.
